analysis.one_liner: Lets cell-based medical therapies be sold to patients for five years without full clinical trials proving they work.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee until the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The REGROW Act would create a fast track for "cellular therapies" — treatments made from human cells, including stem cell products. Companies could sell these therapies for five years after showing only preliminary evidence of safety and no proof they actually work, then apply for full FDA approval. It would also loosen rules for the medical devices used to harvest, process, and deliver these cells, letting them be approved based on lab tests rather than human trials. The bill died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies developing cellular and stem cell therapies gain a shortcut to market: they can sell their products for five years — and potentially longer while the FDA reviews their full application — without conducting the large, expensive phase III clinical trials normally required to prove a treatment works. Makers of the medical devices used to collect, process, and deliver these cells also gain, since their equipment would be approved on lab testing alone and could be used with any cell type.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Cell therapy clinics and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new 'conditional approval' pathway allowing cellular therapy products to be marketed without the large-scale (phase III) clinical trials the FDA normally requires, based on preliminary safety evidence and a 'reasonable expectation of effectiveness'.
Gives sponsors a five-year window to sell the product before submitting a full biologic application, and allows continued marketing even while that application is under review.

Changes medical device rules so that devices used to recover, process, or deliver cellular therapies are approved based on laboratory performance testing rather than human clinical trials, and cannot be restricted to specific cell types unless unique to the device's use.

analysis.who_pays: Patients would pay out of pocket for therapies marketed without proof of efficacy, and could receive treatments that later FDA review finds don't work or have undisclosed risks. Weakened device-testing rules would also mean less evidence behind the equipment used to prepare and deliver the therapies.

drawbacks.text: Products could be sold for five years based on 'preliminary clinical evidence of safety' and only a 'reasonable expectation of effectiveness' — no proof they work — meaning patients could spend money on treatments that a later FDA review might find ineffective.

The bill instructs the FDA to approve cellular-therapy medical devices based on laboratory testing rather than human clinical trials, which reduces the evidence that the equipment used to prepare and deliver these therapies actually works in patients.

If an application submitted after the five-year conditional period is still under review, the Secretary may permit continued marketing — so a product rejected for full approval could keep being sold indefinitely while the review is pending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients with conditions that mainstream medicine cannot treat, faster access to new cell therapies could be a real benefit. But the trade is a weak one: the bill would let products reach the market on preliminary safety evidence alone, with no proof they work, for five years or longer — meaning patients could pay significant sums for therapies that never pan out, while the weakened device-testing rules reduce what is known about the equipment used on them. The delay in definitive trials is a cost of the design itself, not just of the wait.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which referred it to a health subcommittee, and it never got a hearing, a floor vote, or a law.

narrative.text: Introduced on March 16, 2016 by Rep. Mike Coffman with a small bipartisan group of cosponsors (four total).
Two days later it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee, where it remained for the rest of the Congress.
No further action was taken; the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients are spared the risk of paying for unproven cell therapies marketed without efficacy trials; the cell therapy clinics and device makers who would have gained a shortened path to market lose out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients, who avoid paying for unproven therapies

for.name: Rep. Mike Coffman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the REGROW Act on March 16, 2016 and referred it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Reps. Takai (D-HI) and Griffith (R-VA)
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, making it one of the original cosponsors alongside Coffman.

for.name: 4 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Added their names in support of the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or advanced it to the floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call positions were recorded; its handful of cosponsors included both Republicans and a Democrat.

industries.industry: Cellular therapy and stem cell clinics
industries.note: The bill creates a shortcut to market: cell therapy products could be sold to patients for five years without the large clinical trials normally required, then possibly longer while the full application is pending. Patient payments would flow to these businesses without evidence of efficacy.

industries.industry: Medical device makers (cell processing and delivery equipment)
industries.note: Devices used in cellular therapy would be approved based on lab testing rather than human trials and could not be limited to specific cell types, lowering the cost and burden of getting equipment to market.

industries.industry: Cord blood banks, tissue banks, and bone marrow repositories
industries.note: They would gain a new role as cell suppliers for conditionally approved therapies, but must be in full compliance with federal good-tissue-practice rules to participate.

industries.industry: Traditional pharmaceutical and biotech drug developers
industries.note: A new class of competitors could reach the market on far less evidence than established drug approval requires, though the bill preserves all existing FDA pathways unchanged.
